title: Month Calendar
context: Grade 5, the pages on the calendar. An adult sees a page of a wall calendar. What the pages are doing is making the columns of a calendar the days of the week, so that dates in one column are 7 apart, and making one month run on into the next with its days of the week carried over.

writeup.why: Use the days of a week, a fortnight and the months, tell a leap year by its February, read the dates and days of a month's calendar, and carry the days of the week on into the next month.
writeup.look: A month calendar of seven columns from Monday to Sunday, a year strip of twelve month cards, a February card that gains a 29th cell, and a violet jump that goes down a column.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Month Calendar' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of dates placed. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The month calendar fills the left of the area at x 90, y 230, 700 wide, in seven columns each 100 wide, headed Monday to Sunday in ink, with the dates in rows beneath, each row 64 tall. A date the question gives is dropped into its cell in deep blue, labelled Given, and the column of a date is lit amber. A violet jump, labelled Jump, is dragged down a column from one date to the date 7 days on. On the first phase the year strip of twelve month cards runs along y 650, each card 90 wide, and a card is tapped to show whether its month has 31 days or 30. On the second phase the February card of 28 cells stands at x 850, y 240 and a 29th cell is added to it for a leap year, the strip of the years between 2000 and 2099 runs along y 650, and the century bar stands at x 850, y 460. On the fourth phase the Next month button stands at x 850, y 230 and the calendar of the next month lies after the first, its first row carrying on from the last row above it. A day of the week or a date found is green, labelled Answer, at x 850, y 620. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and a key for each day name. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The calendar stays as the child left it, with its dates placed, its jumps drawn down the columns and the day of the week beside the answer in green.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the Next month button is pressed, the last row of the month slides left and the first date of the next month drops in under its day, so the calendar seems to run on like a page turning.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet placed. On the first phase one row of seven day cells lies above a year strip of twelve month cards, all face up and unsorted. On the second a February card of 28 cells stands beside a strip of the years between 2000 and 2099. On the third a month calendar of seven columns holds one date in deep blue under its day of the week. On the fourth the calendar of a month stands with the Next month button beside it and the next month's calendar waiting after it. One thing moves, once: the first row of cells, the February card, the date in deep blue or the Next month button gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any month set up from any date, any year picked on the strip, and the next month laid after it. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on weeks, fortnights and months, leap years, reading a month's calendar and carrying on into the next month.
voiceLines: A month calendar, with seven columns waiting for dates.
Count along the row. Which months have thirty days?
Look at the February. Has it a twenty-ninth cell?
Which column is the date in? How far apart are the dates down it?
Take away whole weeks. How many days are left to carry on?
A new month. Fill it in the same way.
Free play. Set any month and lay the next one after it.
Look down the column again. How far apart are the dates?
You built a calendar, found a leap year and carried the days on.

source_tool.description: A month calendar fills the working area with seven columns, one for each day of the week from Monday to Sunday, and the dates of the month in rows beneath them. A date the question gives is dropped in its cell in deep blue, labelled Given. The column of a date is lit amber, and a violet jump, labelled Jump, is dragged down a column from one date to the date 7 days on. On the first phase the days of a week are counted along a row and a fortnight along two rows, and a year strip of twelve month cards is tapped to show which have 31 days and which 30. On the second phase a February card shows 28 cells, and a 29th cell is added for a leap year. A strip of the years between 2000 and 2099 marks every fourth year as a leap year, and a century bar counts 100 years. On the third phase a month is filled in from one date and its day of the week, and the dates in a column are read down. On the fourth phase the calendar of the next month is laid after the first, with the days carried on from the last row into the first row of the next month. A day of the week or a date found is green, labelled Answer. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the dates placed.
source_tool.art_direction: A wall calendar with paper flaps / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look down the column again. How far apart are the dates?
voice.onNext: A new month. Fill it in the same way.
voice.opening: A month calendar, with seven columns waiting for dates.
voice.onFinish: You built a calendar, found a leap year and carried the days on.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Set any month and lay the next one after it.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has found today's date on a real wall calendar and read the dates down its column. The tool is what fills a whole month in from one date and lays the next month after it, which a single printed page cannot.

answer_key.rule: 1 week is 7 days, and a fortnight is 14 days. January, March, May, July, August, October and December have 31 days each, April, June, September and November have 30 days each, and February has 28 days, or 29 in a leap year. A year has 365 days and a leap year 366. Between 2000 and 2099, every fourth year is a leap year, and a year's February can be read for its 29 days. 100 years make a century. The dates in one column of a calendar are 7 apart. A month of 31 days is 4 weeks 3 days, so the next month begins 3 days on in the week. A question that asks which day of the week is answered with a day name.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's marks. A date placed under the wrong day of the week stays, and the column its date belongs to is lit amber. A leap year given 28 days shows the missing 29th cell lit amber. A jump of seven days that lands in the wrong column is left where it fell, and the column it should reach is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 1 week is 7 days, and a fortnight is 2 weeks.
Then add the 3 days: 14 days + 3 days is 17 days.
So a fortnight and 3 days together come to 17 days.
items.question: How many days make a fortnight and 3 more days?
items.checkpoint: 1 week is 7 days, and a fortnight is 14 days.
items.misconception: Taking a fortnight for 12 days because a month has about four weeks.

steps: A year has 365 days, and a leap year has one more, the extra day being 29 February.
Between 2000 and 2099, every fourth year is a leap year, and 2040, 2044 and 2048 are among them.
So its February has 29 days, and the year has 366 days.
items.answer: Yes, 2044 is a leap year, and it has 366 days.
items.question: Is 2044 a leap year, and how many days does that year have?
items.checkpoint: A leap year has one more day, 29 February; between 2000 and 2099, every fourth year is one.
items.misconception: Forgetting the extra day, so a leap year is counted as an ordinary year.

steps: Each column of a calendar is one day of the week, and the dates in a column are 7 apart.
items.question: 1 September 2026 is under Tuesday on a calendar. On which dates are the Tuesdays of September 2026?
items.checkpoint: The dates in one column of a calendar are 7 apart, so add 7 to move down a column.
items.misconception: Counting the dates along a row instead of down a column, so the next Tuesday comes out as 2.

steps: 31 days is 4 weeks 3 days, because 4 x 7 = 28 and 28 + 3 = 31.
4 weeks bring the same day of the week round again, so only the 3 days carry on.
3 days on from a Friday is a Monday: Saturday, Sunday, Monday.
So 31 days after 1 January 2027 is 1 February 2027, and 1 February 2027 is a Monday.
items.question: January 2027 has 31 days and begins on a Friday. On which day of the week does February 2027 begin?
items.checkpoint: A month of 31 days is 4 weeks 3 days, so the next month begins 3 days on in the week.
items.misconception: Carrying on all 31 days round the week one at a time, and losing count on the way.

items.question: How many days does a year have, and how many does a leap year have?
items.final_answer: 365 days, and 366 days in a leap year

items.question: A calendar has 12 under Wednesday. Which date is under Wednesday in the next row?
items.final_answer: 19, because the dates in one column are 7 apart and 12 + 7 = 19

items.question: A month of 31 days begins on a Monday. On which day of the week does the next month begin?
items.final_answer: Thursday, because 31 days is 4 weeks 3 days, and 3 days on from a Monday is a Thursday

items.question: How many months of a year have 31 days, and which month has only 28 or 29 days?
items.final_answer: Seven months have 31 days, and February has 28 or 29 days

items.question: Between 2000 and 2099, is 2050 a leap year?
items.final_answer: No. Between 2000 and 2099 the leap years come every fourth year, 2048 and then 2052, so 2050 is not a leap year

items.question: 1 August 2027 is a Sunday. Which day of the week is 19 August 2027?
items.final_answer: A Thursday, because 15 August 2027 is a Sunday and 19 August 2027 is 4 days on

items.question: February 2028 begins on a Tuesday and has 29 days. On which day of the week does March 2028 begin?
items.final_answer: A Wednesday, because 29 days is 4 weeks 1 day, and 1 March 2028 is a Wednesday

teaching_notes: Keep a real calendar on the wall and read it before any rule is named. Count the months of 31 days on the knuckles of a fist. Dates in one column of a calendar are 7 apart, so add or take away 7 to move a week. Answer a question about the day of the week with a day name, and a question about a date with a date, asked as on which date.
